motion: Does analytic idealism better explain reality than scientific naturalism?

bridges.statement: Analytic idealism explains reality better than scientific naturalism by combining experiential adequacy, empirical compatibility, and ontological economy.
Consciousness is the sole ontological primitive, while physical reality is the appearance of transpersonal mental processes.
Scientific descriptions capture relational and quantitative appearances but cannot identify or derive the intrinsic qualities of reality.
Dissociation supplies an empirically motivated account of individual minds, bodies, and mind-brain dependence within one field of subjectivity.
Idealism accommodates scientific evidence with fewer unsupported ontological commitments than rival naturalistic theories.
Scientific naturalism remains preferable because it offers the best balance of explanatory reach and theoretical commitment.
Mental processes are theoretically identical with appropriately embedded neural processes, without eliminating either vocabulary.
Natural reality requires irreducible explanatory vocabularies across the sciences even when higher-level entities are physically constituted.
Idealism incurs unresolved explanatory costs concerning dissociation, causal structure, and the diversity of mental states.
Empirical results constrain metaphysics but do not establish the idealist interpretation or eliminate unconsidered naturalistic alternatives.

sections.title: Perception, theoretical entities, and external reality
Mind-brain dependence, dissociation, and altered states

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's uninterrupted opening statement begins at event 40.
moves.proposition: Natural reality includes physical, chemical, biological, psychological, and other domains, with knowledge drawn from all sciences and humanities.
moves.inventoryRationale: Defines Oppy's broad scientific naturalism rather than reductive physicalism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: anything like a reduction to physics
that's why i don't want to call myself
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Oppy's opening statement.
moves.proposition: Because reality cannot be exhaustively described in physics vocabulary, Oppy rejects the label physicalist.
moves.inventoryRationale: Preserves the debate's crucial distinction between scientific naturalism and reductive physicalism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what's fundamental is minds and ideas
minds and ideas are light and local
in the history of natural reality
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly contrasts his view with idealism.
moves.proposition: Idealism makes minds fundamental, whereas naturalism treats minds and ideas as late, local developments in natural history.
moves.inventoryRationale: States the opening metaphysical contrast bearing directly on the motion.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup's clearly introduced opening turn starts at event 99.
moves.proposition: Naturalism excludes supernatural intervention and is compatible with nature unfolding spontaneously according to physical regularities.
moves.inventoryRationale: Establishes that analytic idealism is offered as a naturalist rather than supernatural position.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is a field of subjectivity
moves.attributionBasis: Clear uninterrupted portion of Kastrup's opening exposition.
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism posits a fundamental field of simple subjectivity whose excitations are experiences.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides the core positive ontology of analytic idealism.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: an external world outside our individual minds
regardless of whether we like it or not
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Kastrup's opening position.
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism accepts an objective external world outside individual minds that behaves independently of personal wishes.
moves.inventoryRationale: Blocks the misconception that idealism denies external reality while locating perception at the representational level.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: these two things are certainly not equivalent
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly responds to Oppy's use of naturalism.

responseComponents.component: Argues that naturalism names a scientific outlook and should not be reserved for Oppy's non-idealist ontology.
Rejects framing idealism as the contrast class to naturalism because idealism can itself be naturalistic.

moves.proposition: Idealism can be naturalist because naturalism is a scientific outlook, whereas physicalism is a distinct philosophy-of-mind position.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly contests the debate's governing labels while retaining the substantive ontological dispute.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: just are certain kinds of neural states
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly takes the first open-dialogue response.

responseComponents.component: Corrects Kastrup's characterization of the rival view as emergence: mental processes are identified with neural processes rather than produced as a separate byproduct.

moves.proposition: Conscious and other mental states are certain neural states or processes, so Oppy's identity theory is not an emergence theory.
moves.inventoryRationale: Defines the principal naturalist account of mind used throughout the debate.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: give a definition of say cat
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Oppy's response.
moves.proposition: Oppy distinguishes naturalism from physicalism by the vocabulary needed for fundamentals and denies that cats can be defined in fundamental-physics vocabulary.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces Oppy's distinction between physical constitution and reduction of explanatory vocabulary.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's that experience is physical arrangements
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly addresses Oppy's identity and cat claims.

responseComponents.component: Challenges how experience can simply be physical arrangement without an explanatory identity criterion.
Claims tension between identifying experience physically and denying reduction of a cat to physical vocabulary.

moves.proposition: Identifying experience with physical arrangements appears inconsistent with denying that a cat can be reduced to physical properties alone.
moves.inventoryRationale: Frames the first major direct challenge to Oppy's combined identity and anti-reduction positions.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: doing certain kinds of neural processing
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's answer immediately follows Kastrup's question.

responseComponents.component: Explains the proposed identity relationally: experience is neural processing appropriately embedded in a physical environment and evolutionary setting.

moves.proposition: For humans and cats, having experiences just is undergoing the appropriate environmentally embedded neural processing.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies Oppy's substantive identity criterion rather than merely repeating an identity formula.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Oppy's answer.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes theoretical identification from eliminating either mental or neural descriptions.

moves.proposition: Identity theory says mental and neural states are one reality under two descriptions, without eliminating either side of the identification.
moves.inventoryRationale: Clarifies why multiple vocabularies do not contradict ontological identity.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup's uninterrupted response is clearly marked by the toe analogy.

responseComponents.component: Argues that neural identity does not derive the qualitative nuances of experience from neural properties.
Contends that an unexplained identity assertion is no less arbitrary than identifying consciousness with toe movement.

moves.proposition: Because experiential qualities are not deducible from neuronal properties, identifying neuronal firing with experience appears no less arbitrary than the toe identity.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Kastrup's central explanatory-gap objection in an independently assessable form.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: doesn't count in any way against
an inference to the best explanation
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy answers the deducibility challenge directly.

responseComponents.component: Denies that a priori deducibility is required, comparing consciousness with cats and treating identity as an a posteriori inference to the best explanation.

moves.proposition: Failure of a priori deduction does not count against an entity or identity; mind-brain identity is an a posteriori inference to the best explanation.
moves.inventoryRationale: Gives Oppy's principal answer to the knowledge and explanatory-gap argument.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: cats are real in the same way
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy resumes after the moderator distinguishes theory from ontological reduction.

responseComponents.component: Resolves the alleged contradiction by separating theory reduction from physical constitution and invoking non-reductive supervenience.

moves.proposition: Cats are wholly constituted by physical particles yet remain equally real, so physical constitution does not itself amount to reduction.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides the mature clarification of Oppy's anti-reduction position.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: different patterns in which that thing can be excited
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup clearly answers Oppy's question about his fundamental ontology.
moves.proposition: Natural diversity consists in different patterns of excitation of one fundamental field of phenomenal consciousness.
moves.inventoryRationale: Specifies how idealism proposes to derive plurality from one primitive.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the body is what those mental processes look like
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Kastrup answer about personal minds and evolution.
moves.proposition: A person is a personal mind whose body is the cross-boundary appearance of its mental processes, all within a primitive field of simple subjectivity.
moves.inventoryRationale: Shows how idealism incorporates biological evolution and embodiment rather than denying them.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup directly answers Oppy's request to define dissociation.

responseComponents.component: Offers dissociation as a mechanism by which apparently late, local minds can arise within fundamentally mental reality.

moves.proposition: Psychiatric dissociation is empirically established and involves one integrated mind seemingly partitioning into centers with distinct experiences, memories, and dispositions.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies the empirical analogue underlying Kastrup's account of individual minds.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: brain activity in the woman's visual cortex
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup clearly narrates an empirical dissociation case.
moves.proposition: A reported 2015 dissociative-identity case linked a blind alter's executive control to disappearance of visual-cortex activity despite open eyes.
moves.inventoryRationale: Gives concrete evidence for the claimed capacity of dissociation to structure perception and brain activity.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we do not have a complete
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly marks a concession and then states his hypothesis.
moves.proposition: Kastrup concedes that no complete, unambiguous conceptual account of dissociation is currently available.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records both an important limitation and the positive biological hypothesis built upon it.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the undifferentiated field actually has differentiation
i still i'm sorry i didn't get
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly responds to Kastrup's dissociation account.

responseComponents.component: Questions how genuine boundaries and differentiation arise within what is presented as one field.
Challenges the still-unclear relation between an individual subject and the universal field.

moves.proposition: The dissociation proposal leaves unclear how a supposedly unified field contains real boundaries and how an individual relates to that field.
moves.inventoryRationale: Captures Oppy's recurring challenge as exposure of a missing explanation, not a contrary theory.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup clearly answers Oppy's challenge about timeless structure.

responseComponents.component: Proposes semantic association, rather than spatial separation, as the structure capable of differentiating the fundamental field.

moves.proposition: A non-spatiotemporal structure of existence can be visualized as an associative database structure.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides Kastrup's positive response to the demand for intelligible structure beneath spacetime.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: probably all the parts of it are causal
i think i understand that part
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly evaluates Kastrup's associative model.

responseComponents.component: Concedes intelligibility to non-temporal associative structure while noting it departs from Oppy's preferred universal causal linkage.

moves.proposition: Oppy accepts that he understands the proposed associative structure, though his own view allows non-temporal reality while retaining causal links throughout.
moves.inventoryRationale: Preserves a genuine concession alongside the remaining theoretical difference.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup clearly responds to Oppy's causal preference.

responseComponents.component: Concedes his own reliance on causal thinking but denies that causation is fundamental, treating it as an epistemic representation of deeper associations.

moves.proposition: Kastrup admits difficulty thinking non-causally but ultimately treats causality as an epistemic account of mind-independent associations, not a fundamental feature.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records a candid concession and the idealist account of causal structure.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: strikes me as much more plausible
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly states his comparative view of quantum interpretations.
moves.proposition: A satisfactory quantum interpretation should recover the common-sense material world through decoherence, which Oppy finds more plausible than idealistic interpretations.
moves.inventoryRationale: States the naturalist preference for continuity between fundamental physics and ordinary material reality.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: doesn't explain how the environment became classical
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup directly responds to Oppy's appeal to decoherence; caption renders the term inconsistently.

responseComponents.component: Argues that decoherence is only an operational account of inaccessible superposition information and presupposes, rather than explains, a classical environment.

moves.proposition: Decoherence assumes an already classical environment, so it is a useful operational tool rather than an explanation of the measurement problem.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly rebuts Oppy's proposed route from quantum theory to the common-sense material world.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: not the thing as it is in itself
moves.attributionBasis: Clear Kastrup exposition of the metaphysical implication he draws from relational quantum mechanics.
moves.proposition: Physical entities are relational measurement appearances—representations of what is measured rather than standalone things in themselves.
moves.inventoryRationale: Connects Kastrup's perceptual ontology to his interpretation of physics.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: where we start is where we have to end up
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly responds after Kastrup's quantum-metaphysical argument.

responseComponents.component: Argues that interpreting material experiments as abolishing the material world undermines the evidential standpoint from which the inference begins.

moves.proposition: A metaphysical interpretation of material experiments should recover the material world and cannot coherently discard the evidential basis on which it relies.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Oppy's epistemic self-undermining objection to Kastrup's quantum inference.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: confident that you're not missing something
much more plausible that we're missing something
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's turn directly answers Kastrup's appeal to decades of experiments.

responseComponents.component: Emphasizes that experimental results require interpretation and may leave unknown theoretical possibilities.
Judges missing theory more plausible than the claimed relational-idealist metaphysical conclusion.

moves.proposition: Experiments do not interpret themselves; unknown theoretical options make it more plausible that something is missing than that relational idealism is established.
moves.inventoryRationale: Articulates Oppy's core underdetermination response to the physics-based case.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: trade-off between keeping your commitments minimal
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly answers the moderator's theory-selection question.
moves.proposition: Metaphysical theories should be compared by trading off minimal commitments against maximal explanatory coverage.
moves.inventoryRationale: States the shared comparison standard Oppy uses to defend scientific naturalism.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup clearly follows with his answer to the same moderator question.
moves.proposition: Metaphysical theories concern what nature is and cannot be directly confirmed or refuted experimentally, although experiments can narrow the field by contradicting their assumptions.
moves.inventoryRationale: Gives Kastrup's nuanced account of empirical constraint without claiming direct experimental proof of idealism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly agrees with the final part of Kastrup's answer.

responseComponents.component: Concedes the shared evidential rule that belief should not outrun decent reasons.

moves.proposition: Oppy agrees that ontological belief should not exceed what available reasons support.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records an important methodological concession shared by both sides.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: conscious processing is going on in your brain
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy directly answers the revived toe analogy.

responseComponents.component: Distinguishes the neural identity from the toe identity by citing data supporting a close experience–neural-processing connection.

moves.proposition: Locating consciousness in the toe would be arbitrary, whereas evidence supports a close connection between experience and neural processing in the brain.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies the empirical discrimination Kastrup demanded between neural and toe identities.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's an appeal to a correlate
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup directly replies to Oppy's evidence from mind-brain connection.

responseComponents.component: Argues that correlations underdetermine identity because idealism also predicts them by treating brain activity as the appearance of experience.

moves.proposition: Mind-brain correlations do not uniquely favor physicalism because idealism can also account for them as appearances of conscious experience.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly addresses the strongest empirical support Oppy offers for identity theory.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we replace reality by a description thereof
pull the territory out of the map
moves.attributionBasis: Clear continuation of Kastrup's reply.

responseComponents.component: Rejects inference to identity as explanatory because quantitative descriptions exclude qualities by construction.
Claims empirical correlation cannot bridge the categorical gap between quantitative neural descriptions and qualitative experience.

moves.proposition: Physicalism replaces reality with a quantitative description that excludes qualities by construction, so deriving qualities from it is like pulling territory from a map.
moves.inventoryRationale: Presents the final and most developed form of Kastrup's map–territory argument.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's short response is clearly attributable despite interruption afterward.

responseComponents.component: Objects that the description/reality distinction applies equally to all theories and therefore does not uniquely undermine naturalism.

moves.proposition: Because every theory, including a physicalist theory, is a description, Oppy sees no differentiating force in the description objection.
moves.inventoryRationale: Captures Oppy's final direct answer before the debate is wound down.

selectionRationale: All thirty-six chronological moves remain distinct and source-required. The reduction section contains one Kastrup move and four Oppy moves because Oppy separately develops identity, constitution, vocabulary, and reduction replies, while Kastrup's later explanatory-gap challenges belong in the qualities section. The dissociation section contains four Kastrup moves and one Oppy move because Kastrup supplies a field model, embodiment account, psychiatric evidence, and a limitation concession, while Oppy advances one recurring boundary challenge. The causal-structure section contains three Kastrup moves and one Oppy move because Kastrup develops and qualifies the associative proposal while Oppy concedes its intelligibility. No move was merged, deleted, duplicated, or reassigned to manufacture symmetry.
